one_liner: LZSS codec whose format is built for branchless SSE4.1 decoding; decodes about 1.3x faster than LZ4HC at similar ratio.
what_it_does: Three block codecs (LZSSE2, LZSSE4, LZSSE8), each a .cpp/.h pair with an extern "C" API: allocate a parse state, call LZSSEn_CompressOptimalParse (levels 1-17) or LZSSEn_CompressFast (LZSSE4/8 only), and decode with LZSSEn_Decompress(input, inputLength, output, outputLength). It is a write-once/read-many alternative to LZ4HC, not an LZ4-compatible format; there is no frame, checksum or streaming layer, and the caller must store the uncompressed size.
how_it_is_fast: The stream is a sequence of 4-bit control nibbles packed 16 bytes at a time; the decoder loads one control block, uses pshufb (_mm_shuffle_epi8) lookup tables, compare masks and blendv to compute per-step input and output byte counts and literal/match selection, then each step does an unconditional 16-byte load of the match source, masks in literals and writes 16 bytes, with no data-dependent branches. Matches are short (LZSSE8: 4-byte minimum, up to 15 bytes per control, longer matches chained by carry nibbles) and offsets are 16-bit, so copies stay in a 64 KiB window and in L1/L2. Ratio comes from the optimal parser (binary-tree match finder similar to LzFind plus a Storer-Szymanski style parse), which is why compression is slow.
when_to_use: Assets or data blobs compressed once offline and decompressed many times on x86-64 (games, read-only stores), where decode MB/s matters more than encode time.
Text and mixed corpora at LZ4HC-class ratio: lzsse8 -6 on silesia.tar decodes 5007 MB/s at 35.61% vs lz4hc -12 at 3813 MB/s and 36.45% (lzbench 2.4, EPYC 9555P).
Highly compressible text with LZSSE2, which the README recommends for text with short literal runs.
Code that can vendor a small BSD-2-Clause C++ source drop and wants decode speed with steady per-file throughput.
when_not_to_use: Anything that compresses at runtime: optimal-parse levels run at about 8-9 MB/s, and the only fast mode in lzbench (lzsse4fast, 266 MB/s, 45.26%) is slower and worse than plain LZ4 (550 MB/s, 47.60%, 3832 MB/s decode) on the same run.
Non-x86 targets: requires SSE4.1 and 64-bit x86; no ARM/NEON or scalar fallback (issue #1 'Portable version' open since 2016), and the header warns it performs poorly on 32-bit x86.
LZSSE8 fast-parse output: issue #14 (open, labelled bug, March 2025) has a reproducible file whose LZSSE8_CompressFast output fails to decompress; lzbench flags the same bug.
Untrusted input or tight buffers: issue #7 (open since 2016) reports LZSSE2_Decompress writing outside the buffer for very short data under AddressSanitizer.
Projects needing a maintained dependency: last commit 2019-04-18, 25 commits, and the README itself says the code is only 'approaching production readiness'.

integration.min_toolchain: C++ compiler with SSE4.1 enabled (e.g. -msse4.1): MSVC, Clang or GCC; any other compiler hits '#error Platform not supported'; premake4 project for the example
integration.platforms: x86-64 with SSE4.1 only (lzbench: Windows builds via MinGW-w64 only)
integration.thread_safety: Per the header: one parse state must not be used by concurrent calls; separate states may run in parallel. Decompress is stateless.

gotchas: Decompress expects outputLength to equal the original size: issue #16 (open, Jan 2026) shows LZSSE8 level-17 data decoded into a buffer 32 bytes larger returns 15 bytes short, and issue #12 shows the same for LZSSE2 when the block buffer exceeds the input.
Decompress returns a byte count below outputLength on error rather than an error code, and does no hash check; 'corrupt data can still be valid to decompress' per the header.
The optimal-parse state is large: a 2^20-entry hash root table, a binary-tree node array for the 64 KiB window, and an Arrival record per input byte sized by MakeOptimalParseState(bufferSize).
Compressed output is never larger than the input (stored raw instead), but outputLength for compression must be at least inputLength or the call returns 0.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LZSSE8 over LZ4HC for x86-64-only read-heavy data when about 30% faster decoding at slightly better ratio is worth an unmaintained, SSE4.1-only dependency with open correctness issues; pick LZ4/LZ4HC for portability and maintenance, or misa77 or ZXC for a maintained decode-speed-first codec. LZAV and zstd are better whenever compression speed matters.
verified_claims_summary: In lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar), lzsse8 2019-04-18 -6 decompressed at 5007 MB/s for 35.61% and lzsse4 -6 at 4714 MB/s for 35.91%, vs lz4hc 1.10.0 -12 at 3813 MB/s for 36.45% (1.31x and 1.24x, derived from page data); both LZSSE rows compress at about 9 MB/s, and lzsse2 -6 (3850 MB/s) is level with plain lz4 (3832 MB/s). The author's 2016 blog benchmarks are on a blocked host; a search snippet says LZSSE8 decode stays above 2607 MB/s on binary data where LZ4 dropped to 2115 MB/s on enwik8 (snippet only).
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-04-18 (151 stars, open bug reports from 2016 to 2026 unanswered); BSD-2-Clause and small enough to vendor, but fuzz and round-trip test it yourself and avoid LZSSE8_CompressFast.
